This has nothing at all to do with family allowances. Are you arguing that family allowances is a gift from the Liberal party to the people of Canada, or are they not given by right to the people of Canada by the parliament of Canada? Family allowances or no family allowances, what we say is that those who are primarily responsible for the production of wealth, goods and services in this country are getting virtually nothing. That is not quite right. They get a slap in the face. Corporations are allowed to start their tax reductions on January 1 of this year, while the individual taxpayer cannot start until July 1.
The Budget-Mr. Murphy
In Winnipeg there are 19,000 heads of families earning less than $2,000 a year. With prices where they are, how such a man can clothe his family properly, give them sufficient shelter and the adequate food which our own Department of National Health and Welfare thinks is necessary, is completely beyond the scope of my imagination. If help was required by the majority of people in Canada, surely it would have been advisable to give it by means of a cut in the sales tax and so provide benefits right across the board. Just the other day the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance told us that an average family might save as much as $15 a year had there been a 2 per cent cut in the sales tax. But the government did not choose to do this because it has no social conscience. It has no regard really for the needs of the mass of the people who are earning under $3,000 a year, and they amount to 75 per cent of the heads of families in this country. There has been no help given to them. It may be argued that they are getting some remission on the cigarette tax, but the people who smoke cigarettes are not those in the lower income categories in this country.
When one examines the whole budget, it is the sort of budget on which I should be delighted to fight an election. I can only hope that the government will defer the election as long as possible, because the longer they put it off the more certain is their defeat, and that will be welcomed by a great number of people in this country. Defeat would be appropriate, for if this is justice then it is harsh justice. If this budget is justice, it is capitalist justice. If this be justice, "then judgment has fled to brutish beasts and men have lost their reason."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the time of the house for a few minutes to discuss some aspects of the budget. First of all I want to refer to a situation which exists in my riding, and which I think can be found in several ridings in Canada. We are very fortunate in having a crown company, the Polymer Corporation, which was no small factor in the winning of the last war. It was established at that time because of our shortage of raw rubber. I have at all times paid tribute to the foresight of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and I make no apology for repeating that tribute in the house now because with that particular industry we have become more or less independent of raw rubber in Canada.
The point I wish to make concerning crown companies is this. Unfortunately we

The Budget-Mr. Murphy have had in Canada a more or less archaic law exempting federal property in any municipality from taxation, and not even providing for payments in lieu of taxes. In the fall of 1949 the present government, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), announced a government formula whereby crown companies in any part of Canada were obligated to come to an agreement with the municipalities in which they were situated on a basis that was fair and equitable. I should like to say now that I have praised that formula in the past. As I have said, the Polymer Corporation is in my constituency, and almost from the time I first came into the house, realizing the obligations falling on the different municipalities surrounding that corporation, I urged that some relief be given to them because of the increased cost of roads, schools and everything else involved in municipal administration.
It seemed to me that for several years I pursued a rather lonesome course because I do not recall any support for the idea; and I was greatly relieved, as were the taxpayers of Sarnia, when this formula was announced in the fall of 1949. This same formula applies to other municipalities in Canada, and in the current year the Polymer Corporation, which was formerly in the township of Sarnia, will be paying to the Sarnia municipal treasury some $260,000 odd. Last year the amount was $125,000 and the year before it was $45,000. That was the first year the corporation was in the city of Sarnia. Prior to that it was in the township of Sarnia, and I think it paid $25,000.
It is true that the Polymer Corporation appealed against their assessment this year, as did many other taxpayers in the city, but only a few days ago they announced the withdrawal of their appeal, and I understand that they are prepared to accept the assessment of the city assessor. In all fairness may I say that I think industries and other sizeable properties in Sarnia have received fair consideration because the city did bring in an experienced and well-recognized firm of engineers to deal with the problem of re-assessing property in the city of Sarnia.
What I have said applies to the city of Sarnia, and we are benefiting this year to that extent. It represents a good deal of money, but may I say that I have contended over the years since I have been in the house that crown companies should assume their responsibility in any municipality because they demand the same services that private or other public corporations require.
I do hope that principle will be further extended. I think every hon. member will


agree with me when I say that municipalities in Canada today find themselves in very dire circumstances because of the limited field within which they can obtain revenue. I have said before in the house, and I regret to have to say it again, that the time is almost approaching when it is hardly desirable for a man to own property in some cities because of high municipal taxes.
While we in Sarnia are going to get some $260,000 from this particular crown corporation, I hope other municipalities that have crown corporations will receive similar treatment from such crown companies in their municipalities. It may be that they will be subject to some pressure, but I think the government formula is acceptable to industry. I am happy to see that this particular crown company, of which I am so proud, has accepted that formula; and while they did not pay the same amount in 1950 or 1951 I can say that the management of the Polymer Corporation have now recognized their responsibility to the city of Sarnia and the city of Sarnia is grateful for that recognition, feeling that they are entitled to what they are to receive.
However, they have not gone quite far enough. I do not think any member of the house will disagree with my viewpoint when I say that crown property can be found today in most cities or municipalities in Canada, and it does not seem fair to me, nor do I think it would to any hon. member, to have two properties, one across the corner from the other, one being owned by the federal government and the other being owned by commercial people, both performing the same service, but inasmuch as one does not come within the 4 per cent formula the municipality does not get any revenue from the federal government.
I think today that governments on the high level must recognize the serious situation in which municipalities find themselves. They should, in all fairness to a municipality, give assistance in the way of relief. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of where federal property may be in the Dominion of Canada it should be subject to the same formula that applies to crown corporations. I do not think there is anything wrong with that suggestion. I am going to say that when this debate on the budget is finished and when the resolutions are being considered, it is the responsibility of the government to bring in the necessary amendments in order that relief may be given now.
I do not like the spectacle of the government refusing to give relief now in the form of payment of municipal taxes on federal

property and relief from sales tax on purchases by municipalities-I intend to deal with that later-and three or four months hence on the political platform promising to do these things if it is returned to power. We have had enough of that in the past, and I say let us have action now, Mr. Speaker. We can do it this session, and probably in the next week or ten days. I repeat that the time for action is now.
It has been customary in the past to make changes and I hope that the minister will consider these proposed changes at this time. I repeat:	Do not defer these necessary
courses of action, essential to relieve a serious situation affecting municipalities of this country, until the eve of an election, three or four months hence, and then hope to buy your way back into power by promising what I am sure is justified in the opinion of all individual members of this parliament, regardless of party. Action should be taken now.
I want to pursue this argument a little further because I think it is to the interest of every member in the house. Several members have already commented on it, and yesterday we heard a most interesting speech by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), who quoted facts and figures which were a revelation to me and, I think, to all members. He gave illustrations which pointed out the necessity at this time for some action by the government to relieve municipalities of sales tax. Various members of our party have gone on record to that effect and it seems like repeating, Mr. Speaker, but I do not mind repeating facts such as these if repeating them may mean action by this government at this session. It oftens happens that these sound arguments bear repetition.
I am going to say, and I think I express the opinion of every member in the house, that in each constituency there are cities and towns which are faced with the necessity of buying large quantities of material in order to keep up with the ordinary level of administration. Those purchases are subject to the payment of sales tax. We do exempt provincial governments from sales tax, so I think we have a sound precedent. I hope the government will take action now and not wait until the eve of an election to promise relief for the municipalities. As I said a while ago, it can be done on the resolutions.
A few moments ago I was in touch with our city manager, and he told me that he thought purchases by the city of Sarnia last year which would be subject to sales tax were about $1 million. I will say, Mr. The Budget-Mr. Murphy Speaker, that I expected a telegram confirming the statement before this moment, but there must be municipalities in Canada whose purchases, subject to sales tax, would amount to a great deal more. Mr. Speaker, in these days there must be some relief for those municipalities and 1 would hope that, before the resolutions are finally disposed of, the necessary amendments can be made so relief may be brought to municipalities from this form of taxation, which I think is very unfair. I do not believe any member in the house will quarrel with that statement.
The figures have been quoted before by the leader of my party and by our financial critic when he was referring to revenue from the taxation dollar as it was divided by different levels of government. I think it is awfully important that the figures really sink in because they are astounding and astonishing. If there is a trend here something is bound to happen, and something is bound to crack. In 1939 the federal government took 51 cents, the provincial government 19 cents and the municipalities 30 cents of the taxation dollar. In 1952 the federal government takes 77 cents, the provincial government 12 cents, and the municipalities 11 cents.
Mr. Speaker, in 13 years the municipalities have lost the difference between 30 cents and 11 cents of every dollar, practically two-thirds of the revenue they were collecting. This cannot go on. It is no wonder that municipalities today are crying through their provincial governments to have a dominion-provincial-municipal conference; because if this thing is to go on, how can they build schools, how can they build highways and streets?
I do not mind admitting to the house today that in the city of Sarnia-and there we have a very progressive city, one that has probably grown faster than any other in Canada during the last five years-our municipal problem is so serious that when we were asked to build and construct a sewage system, we told the federal government that we were not in a position to construct a sewage disposal plant. That is the position we are in.
So far as schools are concerned, we know that we must educate our children. No one in this house or in this country wants our children to suffer from lack of education. The costs are high. True, there are some grants from the provincial governments, but the situation is very difficult as I have found it in my part of the country. I have been through a good deal of the western part of Ontario and those areas are all in the same position. It is becoming unbearable.
2624	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Murphy
I want to say too, Mr. Speaker, that the matter ot municipal taxation does not apply to cities only. I happen to have a little interest in a farm in a township. Four years ago the taxes were $57 but last year they were $197. This problem of taxation applies to farm areas as well as to urban areas. It is no wonder, Mr. Speaker, that there are leaders of provincial governments in this country who have been very much concerned about the situation. As a matter of fact only recently one provincial government appointed a royal commission to inquire into the situation. They have appointed a most responsible body of men to get the viewpoints of the different municipalities. According to the press reports this commission is to inquire into and consider the distribution of tax revenues as between the federal authority, the provinces and municipalities and school boards.
This situation does not apply to one province only, Mr. Speaker; it applies to every province in the dominion. I hope when this commission begins hearing evidence someone here in Ottawa will establish a listening post, because the evidence is bound to reflect the situation which so many of us have painted in the last few days concerning what is happening to the municipalities and the taxpayers in those municipalities. I repeat that if the government did nothing else by way of amending these resolutions-and they have already been amended-but take care of this problem, it would bring relief to the municipalities and would be greatly appreciated not only by those municipalities but by every member in this house.
By way of further argument, may I say that the various cities in this country have co-operated with the provincial and dominion authorities in respect to civil defence. It is true that many people believe civil defence is a matter within federal jurisdiction. After all is said and done, however, the municipalities have agreed to co-operate with the higher levels of government. They have pledged themselves to purchase equipment in order to play their part in civil defence. I wish to point out something that does not coincide with my idea of fair play. The municipalities are obliged to pay sales tax on the equipment they purchase. I do not think that is fair, and I do not think the municipalities believe it is fair.
There are a few other matters which I wish to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker. The budget resulted in a decrease in the duty on cigarettes. Reference has been made to this matter by other speakers from this party. I want to say that since I came


into this house I have made speeches advocating that the tax on cigarettes be reduced. I live near the border and, as a matter of fact, was in the tobacco business, wholesale, retail and manufacturing, and I know the impact caused by a cheaper cigarette in the United States. I advocated continually that the tax be reduced. As a matter of fact when this government increased the tax, Hansard will record my statement informing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that his revenue would be reduced because of the law of diminishing returns. He said he thought he was doing fairly well, but as a matter of fact he did not do so well, as the figures prove. I still say that so much of our population lies close to the border that, in the interests of the revenue of this country as well as the tobacco industry as a whole, the tax might well be reduced another $1.50 per thousand. When I say that, I am thinking of the tobacco grower as well.
Statements have been made before to the effect that no relief has been granted to the pipe smoker. This is true, but I hope even that may be reconsidered before the resolutions are finally voted upon. It is not everyone who can afford to smoke cigarettes at the price they are today, and many people do enjoy a pipe or even rolling their own cigarettes.
The radio tax has been removed. I have no hesitation in saying here that I, along with several members of our party, have advocated the removal of that nuisance tax ever since I have been in the House of Commons. I shall not make any reference now to the suggested tax on television, because I hope that will never appear on the statute books of Canada.
We have in Sarnia, as have many other municipalities, a number of employees working for the federal authority. There are the customs and immigration men, post office workers and so on. In this chemical valley most employees are on the five-day week. The banks are open for only an hour on Saturday, but I understand they are going to be closed all day before too long. I hope the government will give serious consideration at an early date to seeing that these civil servants are placed on a five-day week.
In Sarnia we are very proud of these customs people. I should not single them out, but for this purpose I will. The first people the United States tourist encounters when crossing into Canada are the customs and immigration men. It is important that we have good men. I want to tell the minister that he can well be proud of the officers, not only in the customs branch but

also in the immigration branch. This has been brought to my attention by many people who have had occasion to interview them when crossing into Canada.
Because of the publicity Sarnia has obtained as a result of the huge development of the chemical industry there, I want to mention some facts today which might be of interest to hon. members. Construction to the value of about $50 million is now taking place, and that is not a small amount even with the dollar worth only a few pennies. I hope that some time this year the members of the house will have an opportunity of visiting Sarnia. I would be very glad to see that they are properly taken care of, if such a visit could be arranged. Possibly there could be a boat trip to Detroit for a ball game, and then a tour of this industrial empire. I am not paying for it, and I shall tell you that now if you are looking around at me.
We do have industries there in which many people are interested. We receive Alberta oil. We have the Polymer Corporation. The Sun Oil Company is now constructing a $30 million refinery which will be in operation this fall. The Canadian Oil Company has just finished a $30 million refinery. Just this week Imperial Oil allocated another	several	millions for
improvements, in addition to the $14 million project now under way. I am mentioning these figures because they are important, and I believe many members would find a visit to Sarnia very interesting. I hope something of that sort can be arranged.
There is another point with respect to this particular area with which I should like to deal in the little time I have left at my disposal. We have under consideration by this parliament the St. Lawrence seaway scheme. I should like the house to know that 19,000 ships passed Sarnia in 1952. That may sound like an astounding figure, nevertheless it is a fact. I am sure that when the St. Lawrence seaway is completed that figure will be increased in no small measure. We have also, of course, the Blue Water bridge. Across that bridge last year came 910,000 automobiles. It is no wonder that I have always been interested in the tourist industry in Canada. I hope at a later date to make some contribution to that debate.
Mr. Speaker, I have just had handed to me a note which I wish to place on the record. It was a phone message and is to the effect that Sarnia's purchases subject to sales tax were $606,689, and their sales tax on that amount was slightly over $60,000 in 1952. That is not peanuts for any 08108-1674
The Budget-Mr. Murphy municipality. It is true enough that in my area we have a crown company but I have made out my case in the past, and I need not repeat it now, that they are making their contribution to the municipality. I think the greatest relief the government could give to the municipalities of this country, on the basis of these figures, would be to cut out the sales tax on any purchases made by any municipality in Canada.
The people out our way are, as they are all across Canada, concerned naturally about the budget. They woke up two or three days after its delivery and had a different opinion of it. It is true enough that they may have had a wrong impression the night of its delivery or the next day; but looking at it as they do now, accepting the bare facts as presented by the budget and realizing what their income is, they are disillusioned. Many of them are disappointed.
I want to say here that while the employees in Sarnia are drawing the second highest daily or weekly wage in the province of Ontario, there are many people outside of the city of Sarnia who do not enjoy that particular standard, and they are greatly concerned about the present level of taxation. Take the case of a married man with two dependent children; at $2,400 a year his income tax is reduced $1 this year. Take the man with two children and earning $3,000; he will save $4 this year. I understand that 75 per cent of the earners of this country receive $3,000 or less per annum.
However, we find that a man who may be enjoying, from dividends from Canadian companies, an income of close to $10,000-and who makes not one other contribution to his country except to sit on his big fat fanny and draw those dividends-pays not one single cent to the treasury of Canada. I do not think it is quite fair, Mr. Speaker, that a man drawing $2,000, $2,500 or $3,000 should accept the responsibility of the man who is fortunate enough to be able to draw say $10,000 and contribute nothing to his country.
The farmers in my section of the country are also discouraged. They know that their income is down. I am told that in 1952 the income of the farmers of this country dropped by some $25 million. That is a drop of 12 per cent from 1951. I could go on and mention other figures with respect to^ taxation but my time is limited, and I think our party has made an excellent case.
What concerns the little fellow in the back concession, on the side road and in the small towns and cities is this. What value are we getting for those dollars? They seem to have the idea that they are not getting value; and who can blame them, Mr. Speaker, for
2626	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Murphy getting that idea? Through the press, through the radio and through various committees we have had revealed to us what is taking place, and it is no wonder that the voter back home is just waiting for the opportunity to cast his ballot at the next *election.
They are disturbed when they read of a single nursery getting $250,000 for landscaping some defence property. They wonder whether that is necessary. A tile flooring at Churchill required a contract for over $92,000. They wonder about that sort of thing, because they do not have those things in their own homes. For alterations and additions to the officers' mess at Kingston the bill was $340,000. If the bill was $340,000, and it was warranted, let some evidence be given before this house that that expenditure was warranted and we will accept it.
Even the men in uniform are wondering today what in the world the government is doing with all this money. They are wondering as well as the taxpayers back home; and it is no wonder. We have eight prefabricated buildings in Alberta costing over $1 million. We want to know the size of those prefabricated buildings. We understand it was an enormous price. It is no wonder that we have heard about some 231 contracts on a cost-plus basis amounting to over $106 million. Those are government contracts.
I am going to say to this house right now, Mr. Speaker, that it is not too hard for an individual such as any one of us here to enter into a contract with a contractor, on a cost-plus basis, to build a home or a building, because we can give it the necessary supervision. But when the government does this sort of thing and spends the taxpayers' money, they certainly do not get value for that money. That fact has been admitted by senior officials of the government.
We find here 25 contracts for landscaping various government buildings at a cost of more than $1 million. At Wainwright, Alberta, for a swimming pool, $22,000 was spent; for a gymnasium, $280,000. For water at this camp, $1,830,000 was spent; at Whitehorse, $701,000 to erect 30 prefabricated houses. I know a little bit about building homes, Mr. Speaker, and I would love to get one of those contracts. If I did, I think I could retire from the House of Commons.
Five hundred huts were built at Bouchard, Quebec, for $3,555,000. They were not houses; they were huts. In my opinion, that is ridiculous. That works out at over $7,000 a hut. The sum of $314,000 was spent to


replace sub-floors in various R.C.A.F. buildings at Greenwood. Construction of a single mess at Camp Borden cost $560,000.

I do not mind the interruptions, Mr. Speaker; I just love them.
This year the United Kingdom is to spend $4,478 million for defence, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). This certainly impressed me, as I am sure it impressed all hon. members. Over there they have 880,000 people in uniform. We expect to spend about $2 billion, and we have about 100,000 in uniform. In other words we spend about half as much as they do, but we receive for that expenditure only about one-ninth as much.
No wonder the men in the services are disturbed; because after all is said and done, they do not get their dollars too easily. They, too, would like to save for tomorrow. I doubt, too, whether the small wage earners in this country will ever be in a position to save money, so long as this government is in power.
Inasmuch as my constituency is on the route of the seaway, and due to the fact that in a debate of this kind one may deal with a variety of subjects, let me say that we on this side of the house are most enthusiastic

about not only the start of the seaway project but also its completion. The minister is not in his seat at the moment, but I have brought up this matter before. I understand $300,000 has been set aside this year for harbour improvements at Sarnia. My suggestion would be that, inasmuch as the seaway project is almost under way, any harbour improvements along the 2,000 miles of the system should have regard to the whole system, if and when it is completed. I am one who believes firmly that there are some parts along that system which will be, so to speak, a second Ruhr. Those of us in Sarnia, along lake Huron, and especially along the river St. Clair, will probably find ourselves in what I have described as a second Ruhr in this country, because in that area we have those facilities so necessary for successful production.
As has been admitted by the authorities, we are the centre of the refining industry in Canada. With the projection of the facilities of the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company from Superior to Sarnia, with a capacity of
300.000	barrels a day, we have before us no small project. I think the planners of that project have in mind a greater and bigger Ontario, because in view of our recent expansion our refining capacity today is almost
100.000	barrels per day. I feel, however, that the possibility of a refining capacity of 300,000 barrels per day may be some distance in the future, so far as Sarnia is concerned.
With the output of this pipe line coming to Sarnia I believe Sarnia may become one of the first outlets into the United States for Canadian crude oil. Because of the low tariff on Canadian oil entering the United States I believe that we in the Sarnia area are in a position to compete with oil produced in that country. I would hope that before too many years roll along we could supply the great demand in Detroit, Cleveland and Toledo with oil from western Canada.
I think it unnecessary to speak at greater length at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments and suggestions on the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
But first, I wish to call to mind the coronation of our gracious sovereign, Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada. The county of Chapleau, which I represent, is probably the youngest in the country, but it is made up mainly of Canadians who have been in this country for generations. While learning to love their country, they have also learned to respect authority, of which the crown is
The Budget-Mr. D. Gourd the highest symbol. Therefore, I rejoice that the coronation is to take place this year and I congratulate particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for his statesmanship in taking the necessary steps so that our queen may bear a title showing what she is truly for us: the Queen of Canada.
I listened to the remarks of the members of the opposition on the budget and found their criticism both destructive and inconsistent. This government, since it has been in power, has enacted various social welfare measures in order to give assistance to the less favoured classes, to those who need the help of the country and deserve it, while protecting always private enterprise.
The same people who criticized the government for having enacted family allowances and anti-inflation measures, in order to protect the less favoured classes against the rising cost of living, are today blaming it for granting tax relief to corporations, alleging obviously without sincerity that the tax reductions should have been granted mostly to the people in the lower income brackets.
The social security legislation enacted by this government shows that before anyone else, better than anyone else and in spite of the opposition of any other party, it is aware of the needs of the people and is concerned about it. Nevertheless this country has become great under a system of free enterprise and private initiative which is so much in accordance with Christian tradition and which constitutes our best defence against communism. Our government must see to it that private enterprise is encouraged. There is no better way of ensuring that those of more modest means, wage earners for the most part, will actually receive their salary which will rise as these private businesses develop along with the country.
Instead of attacking those reductions which were necessary for the development of the industries on which the prosperity of this country depends, the opposition should realize that the budget not only brings about an 11 per cent reduction in personal income tax which directly favours low income Canadians, but that it is directly favourable to the consumer in several cases, for instance through the abolition of the stamp tax on cheques, of radio licences, the reduction of the tax on cigarettes, etc.
I will give an example which shows that the low income groups of taxpayers are not as badly treated as the opposition would have us believe.
A married taxpayer, with two children and an income of $2,400 a year, will pay $15 in income tax, but will receive $135 in family

The Budget-Mr. D. Gourd allowances. This bonus of $135 is being added to his income of $2,400, and so on, according to the increase in family allowances. However, a taxpayer whose income is $50,000 a year, will pay $21,000 in income tax and the one whose income is $200,000 a year will pay $125,000.
I wish to point out that in my constituency, thanks to the Family Allowances Act, the government has paid yearly to those who have children, and who consequently need it most, the sum of $1,450,000 for 20,000 children. To our citizens in the 70-year-old category, the government has paid $900,000 to 1,875 persons and $100,000 to those between 65 and 69. In pensions to the blind, it has paid out nearly $15,400 to about 30 people.
Under the national health program, the government has also contributed $196,723.02 for the erection of the Hotel-Dieu hospital of Amos, as well as $291,138.82 for the erection of the Macamic sanatorium, not to mention $167,435.43 granted to the organization which looks after tuberculosis control.
Another group of the opposition takes us to task for not having socialized business concerns in this country. What better evidence is there that Canada was right in not indulging in socialistic experiments, which have failed elsewhere, than the political, economical and social stability and prosperity which this government has been able to give the country. The Canadian government has been able to reduce the national debt, from 1946 to 1953, by $2,285,000,000. Moreover, the Hon. Minister ox Finance has been able to reduce taxes, since 1949, by $350 million, not to mention the fact that our dollar is at the present time the soundest in the world, in spite of the tremendous amount of money which it was necessary to earmark for the building up of our defence against our outside enemies, and more particularly against communism. On this occasion, I congratulate the Right Hon. the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), as well as the head of the Canadian delegation to the United Nations, the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I congratulate them for the part they have played as Canadian representatives, in the common allied effort, directed against the menace of communism, war and invasions, more particularly as regards the Atlantic pact organization and of the union of western countries. We naturally hope that, in a foreseeable future, the peril of communism shall have lessened sufficiently to enable us to reduce our national defence

expenditures, in order to spend larger sums for the development of our national resources, as well as for social welfare, more particularly for family allowances, old age pensions and help to the crippled and the disabled.
May I, at this point, urge the government to take the steps which are necessary to create a diversified market for our surplus production. My impression is that Canada has to sell to other countries about 40 per cent of its production. We have had, in that connection, many unhappy experiences. More recently, the monetary situation of the sterling countries, that of Great Britain especially, has created difficulties which justify the suggestion which I am now making. I praise the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) for the efforts he made in that connection recently, on his good-will trip to South America.
Mr. Speaker, the Chapleau riding which I represent is one of the largest in size and one of the most important in respect to natural resources, such as timber stands, mines, hydroelectric power as well as agriculture and dairying. That same riding is certainly one of the most important of all on account of the development which it is now undergoing and of its increase in population. The Canadian National Railways line crosses it from east to west, from Rapide Blanc to the Ontario border, the distance between those points being 365 miles. In the north-south direction, my riding is at least 200 miles long. I need hardly say that in such a vast area, the rapid utilization of our natural resources and the increase in population have created many urgent needs. Since I have been elected to represent the riding, the government have improved the facilities of the Canadian National Railways; stations have been repaired, a new one having been built at Senneterre, an important junction point. They have repaired or built post offices. They are organizing a rural mail delivery system, which will soon come into operation. They have installed, for our national defence, radar equipment at Senneterre and Parent. Rivers have been dredged in order to prevent floods, many wharves have been built or repaired along our lakes and rivers. Many buildings have been completed, cr improved wherever they were most appropriate for the welfare of our Indians. A school will soon be built in my riding to facilitate their education, the measure being one of many which the government is taking in order to raise the standard of living of the Indians both from

the educational and the financial points of view. Moreover, the government has given substantial assistance to hospitals and sanatoria in the county; it has also made certain grants for warehouses and, in order to help the agricultural people, it is also prepared to give subsidies, as provided for in the Cold Storage Act. Such facilities are urgently needed owing to the large agricultural production of Chapleau county. We encourage farmers' study groups, the agricultural society, the co-operative societies and public bodies to endeavour to obtain as much as possible by way of grants for the construction of cold storage plants.
If we take into account the size of my constituency and its natural resources, we can say that the progress made is but a beginning. For instance, when one realizes that the
65,000	people of my riding are living near the railway line that crosses the southern part of my county, it is easy to foresee the possibility of establishing hundreds of new parishes, that will add thousands of people to our population, as soon as we have the required transport facilities. We will need roads and railways. To cope with the needs, a railway has been built from Barraute to Beattyville; taking into account the distance it covers, it is the most profitable line in Canada.
Unfortunately, the extension of this railway from Beattyville to Chibougamau, is now long overdue; this delay is detrimental to the development of our forest, mineral and hydroelectric resources. There are at present along the proposed route of this trunk line, between Beattyville and Chibougamau, at least 80 mining companies, a great number of which are in operation while other companies are ready to start operations. I would like to mention, in particular, the Opemiska Mining-a subsidiary of Dome Mines-Chibougamau Explorers, Campbell Chibougamau and Merill Island.
Most of those companies have to resort to airplanes for the greatest part of their transportation. Moreover, the Opemiska Company is sending every day by road 80 tons of concentrates from Chibougamau to St. Felicien and, by rail, from St. Felicien to Noranda, to the Noranda smelting works, a distance of 800 miles which could be cut down to 300 miles and, according to the statistics I have consulted, the companies now operating at Chibougamau could ship by the new railway, through the trunk line I have suggested, a minimum of from 300 to 400 tons of concentrates a day to the Noranda smelting works.
This is only one aspect of the necessities, and of the revenues which justify the construction of this extension. There would be
The Budget-Mr. D. Gourd added the hauling of ordinary freight and thousands of feet of dressed lumber and millions of cords of pulp wood.
According to certain experts, the construction of these 164 miles of trackage 'would cost approximately from $85,000 to $90,000 per mile, which gives a total of $14 to $15 million. The annual operating costs and the interest charges would reach approximately $4 million. The same experts predict that the revenue which would be derived from the mining and lumber concerns: now interested in the possibilities of this area would be a little over $5 million. This would seem to ensure a revenue from the very beginning of operations for the railway line in question. Along with further development, it could be expected that the revenue would increase.
Mr. Speaker, I have already indicated to the house the various reasons of national importance which would justify this government taking up with the Ontario government the matter of completing the road between Norembega, in the latter province, and the town of La Reine, in Quebec, a distance of 47 miles. It is not my intention to repeat these arguments; I do believe, however, that the dangers threatening our country and the invention of modern weapons which have justified the establishment of a screen of radar stations, two of which are located in my constituency, require direct action on the part of the Department of National Defence in order to complete this road and establish a communication system between the two provinces. In a time of emergency and of national danger, if transportation by railway should become impossible, the situation would be ridiculous. It would be necessary to go down from La Reine to Rouyn-Noranda, a distance of about 100 miles, and from Noranda cross over to Ontario, take the Cochrane road and come back to Norembega, a total distance of over 500 miles. In other words, communications would be impossible.
We therefore suggest that the Department of National Defence should see to it that this distance of 47 miles along the border of the two provinces be linked at once by a direct road.
On numerous occasions, Mr. Speaker, I have suggested that the federal government should help our gold-mining industry, which is in dire straits because gold is selling at a fixed price, whereas labour, materials and equipment necessary to produce gold have all undergone tremendous price increases.
The government must, of course, proceed with caution, and I congratulate them for what they did in this regard a few months ago. I suggest however that they consider

The Budget-Mr. D. Gourd this question once more, in view of recent developments in that field, and that new steps be taken in order to cope with the further needs of the mining industry.
I would not want to resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, without mentioning once again, as I did in my recent speeches, the necessity for Canada to be represented at the Vatican state.
Well-nigh all the countries of the world have their representatives in that state; moreover, the whole universe recognizes, without any religious or national prejudice, that the Holy See is a factor of union and of peace between nations; that is why I am convinced that if Canada appointed such a representative it would be a help to our country and a contribution towards world peace.
I submit, moreover, that the present government would comply with the wish of most Canadians and would be following its usual "Canada first" policy if they provided the country with a national flag. We are a sovereign member of the British commonwealth of nations; by virtue of certain amendments to the British North America Act our Supreme Court has become the final judicial authority. The Queen's representative in Canada, the Governor General, is a native-born Canadian. So that it would seem that the creation of a national flag would complete the evolution of Canada.

speechtext: Would the hon. member allow a question?,

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are you suggesting an extension of the highway which now goes from Toronto to the Quebec border and from there to La Reine, in the province of Quebec?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What I have said is this. Norembega is about 22 miles from Cochrane and there are 47 miles between Norembega and La Reine. These 47 miles are therefore in Ontario. Now I explained to the Department of National Defence that if our country should be invaded from the north and certain railway bridges destroyed, no direct means of communication would then be left between the two provinces. I believe that if the province of Ontario does not build that highway, which should have been done long ago, the Department of National Defence should build it. Should there be an invasion and the railway destroyed such a road would be necessary.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 19 last, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made in the house a most interesting budget speech. Needless to say, I do not pretend to qualify as a financial expert


and I would not dare speak in an authoritative way about that document. I shall, however, venture some personal opinions on the budget speech, even though -they may have been voiced already by those who have preceded me in this debate.
In a first chapter entitled "Economic Trends", the Minister of Finance spoke of the commonwealth economic conference held in London last December. The countries member of that group then stated that their aim was, and I quote Hansard at page 2117: ... to secure international agreement on the adoption of policies by creditor and debtor countries which will restore balance in the world economy on the lines of "trade not aid" and will by progressive stages and within reasonable time create an effective multilateral trade and payments system covering the widest possible area.
And I wish to lay more emphasis on the last part of this last sentence:
... an effective multilateral trade and payments system covering the widest possible area.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I endorse with pleasure that statement. I would even go further and say that, if Canada has to make financial and economic sacrifices in order to promote and extend to the greatest possible number of countries that multilateral trade system, it should not hesitate to act along that line. While I am speaking on that subject, I would like to say that I am pleased with the efforts made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in order to increase and diversify our trade relations with Latin American countries. I believe that identical efforts should also be made to obtain the same results with countries in Europe and Asia, even if in trying to achieve that purpose, we would suffer a slight reduction in the volume of our trade with our friendly neighbour, the United States.
Nowadays, we hear a great deal about coalitions of countries, spheres of influence, the iron curtain, etc.-ominous signs of war. A good way to break up such coalitions, which are a threat to peace, would be to extend international trade beyond the protective walls of those countries or groups of countries, provided, of course, that this be physically possible.
We know from history that countries which engage in honest trade-I repeat honest trade-seldom fight one another. As a rule, war threatens only when such countries, for some reason or other, break off their trade relations. From that angle the United Kingdom is perhaps not so much to blame for having kept open her trading post in Hong Kong and for trying to establish commercial relations with the U.S.S.R. It is quite another matter when the United States send gifts to Tito, the dictator; here, transactions are

based on something quite different and they pursue perhaps a different aim.
However, if we are ready to make sacrifices in order to promote international trade, thus hoping to banish the menace of war, those sacrifices should be compensated in our country by a reduction of our defence expenditures. But the minister's recent budget shows that those expenditures will not be reduced by more than $930,000, or less than a million on expenditures totalling $2 billion. How long is Canada going to continue along that road? Have we not now reached the extreme limit which it would be dangerous to exceed, or even to maintain? Have we not come to the point where we are building up external security at the expense of internal security?
I am under no illusions whatever, Mr. Speaker, about the way in which these words will be greeted in almost every political circle, if, indeed, they are not merely contemptibly ignored. It would nevertheless be wise to remind ourselves that the most elaborate budget speeches, the most responsible, the most realistic and, let us say it, the most honest, have not always warned us in time of certain dangers, as cruel as they were unexpected.
And what with this exorbitant, and to me unjustified war budget, we realize with some
The Budget-Mr. Poulin bitterness that the Canadian people will have to pay more taxes in the next year than in the year 1952-53.
Certain rates were changed or reduced, but the amount to be paid is going to increase to such an extent that Canadians will pay next year, in income tax, for example, $1,350 million as against $1,187 million in 1952-1953. In excise tax, $280 million will be paid instead of $257 million; in sales tax, $590 million instead of $568 million. And thus, by way of comparison, Canadians of all classes will pay next year $335 million more in tax than they did this year. If this is made possible through a greater effort on the part of the Canadian people as a whole, the reward for this effort, it will be recognized, will rather smack of bitterness which will perhaps discourage them from keeping it up.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask you to call it six o'clock.
On motion of Mr. Poulin the debate was adjourned.
